title: Stop Work Authority
basis: 29 CFR 1977.12(b)(2) (refusal to work in dangerous conditions) and 29 CFR 1926.20(a)-(b)
summary: Anyone on the crew should be able to stop work that looks unsafe. OSHA rules say what an employer may not require, and set narrow conditions under which a worker's refusal to do dangerous work is protected.
talking_points: No contractor or subcontractor may require a worker to work in surroundings or under conditions that are unsanitary, hazardous or dangerous to health or safety (29 CFR 1926.20(a)).
Unsafe equipment must be tagged or locked out, or removed from service (1926.20(b)(3)). If you find a hazard, tell your supervisor so it can be fixed.

A worker's right to refuse dangerous work under 29 CFR 1977.12(b)(2) is protected only when all four of these are true: there is a real danger of death or serious injury that a reasonable person would see in the same circumstances; you refuse in good faith; there is no reasonable alternative; and there is not enough time, because of the urgency, to get the danger removed through regular enforcement channels.
Where possible, you must also have asked your employer to correct the danger and been unable to get it corrected.
Good practice: use your company's stop-work process first. Stop, make the area safe, report the hazard and do not restart until it is fixed.
site_hazards_to_check: Work continuing near a hazard no one has corrected
Damaged or unsafe equipment still in use
Worker afraid to report a hazard
No named person to call when work is stopped
Restart without checking that the hazard is fixed
discussion_questions: Who do you tell first when you see a hazard, and what happens next?
What would make you stop work on this job today?
What has to be true before we restart after a stop?

flags: Verified 29 CFR 1977.12(b)(2) verbatim on osha.gov: real danger of death or serious injury a reasonable person would see, good-faith refusal, no reasonable alternative, insufficient time for regular enforcement channels, and where possible the employee sought correction from the employer. Talking points 3-4 match.
Verified 1926.20(a) (contractor may not require hazardous/dangerous conditions) and (b)(3) (tag/lock out or remove unsafe equipment).

1977.12 is an OSHA anti-discrimination interpretation (Part 1977), not a 1926 construction standard; no 1926 section states a stop-work right, so this is the appropriate cite. Talk frames refusal protection as narrow and does not promise legal protection.
